opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I hear that critique a lot, and I think it rests on a slightly outdated picture of what a moat looks like in this space.

The classic argument goes: if you're partnering with pharma and the wet-lab data generated in those collaborations mostly belongs to the partner, then you're just a model shop renting out compute and clever architectures, and eventually someone with more proprietary data eats your lunch. There's a kernel of truth there. Data ownership matters, and nobody should pretend otherwise.

But I'd push back on a few things. First, in structure prediction and molecular design, the biggest gains over the last few years haven't come from one company hoarding a private dataset. They've come from how you use the public data: the PDB, sequence databases, and then the modeling choices, training recipes, and inference-time tricks layered on top. The public data is a shared floor. What separates teams is what they build on top of it and how fast they iterate.

Second, partnerships aren't just a data question, they're a feedback-loop question. Even when you don't own the raw assay results, you learn an enormous amount about where your models fail: which target classes are hard, which design proposals don't express, which binding predictions don't hold up in the lab. That tacit knowledge flows back into the next model generation. It's harder to put on a slide than "we have ten million proprietary data points," but in practice it compounds.

Third, there's a distribution and trust moat that people underrate. Getting embedded in real discovery programs at serious companies is slow. You have to prove the models actually move programs forward, integrate with their workflows, pass their internal validation. Once you're in, switching costs are real. That's not a data moat, but it's a moat.

Where I'd concede the point: if you only ever do partnerships and never build any internal experimental capacity or negotiate for some data rights, you are exposed long-term. The smart version of this strategy is a hybrid: partner widely to get real-world signal and revenue, structure deals so some learnings or derived data come back, and selectively generate your own data where the model is weakest.

So I don't think "no data moat" is the right framing. The better question is whether the learning loop is faster than everyone else's. If it is, the moat is the velocity, not the dataset.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on the framing a bit, because "data moat" tends to get used as if it's one thing, and in drug discovery it's really at least three.

The first is the kind of data people usually mean: huge proprietary assay datasets, the thing a big pharma has sitting in a LIMS somewhere. The honest truth is we were never going to win on that axis, and I don't think anyone building a structure model today should pretend they will. Pharma has decades of it, they're not going to hand it over, and even if they did, a lot of it is inconsistent across sites and campaigns in ways that make it less valuable than it looks on a slide.

The second kind is the data you generate by actually running the model against reality. That's where the partnership strategy does the opposite of what the critique says. When we work with a partner, the designs go into the wet lab, and what comes back is a signal about where the model is wrong. That failure data is almost impossible to get any other way, because nobody publishes the hundred binders that didn't bind. You only see that if you're in the loop with people doing the experiments. So I'd argue the partnerships are how you build the moat, not evidence that you lack one.

And the third is the stuff that lives in the model itself and the people around it: how you handle a target with no homologs, how you set up a design campaign so the lab results are interpretable, what you've learned about which metrics actually predict a hit. That compounds. You can't easily copy it even with the same training set.

Where I'd agree with the skeptics is on terms. If you structure partnerships so the partner owns all the readouts and you can't learn from them, then yes, you're just a service shop and the critique is fair. So the question I'd ask of us, or of anyone in this space, isn't "do you have a data moat" but "do your contracts let the model get smarter from the work." If the answer is yes, the partnership strategy is the moat. If it's no, you don't have one, regardless of what's on your cap table.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim conflates a partnership model with a particular set of data rights. The important question is what comes back from the partnership: Do you get experimental results? Do you get to learn from the failures as well as the successes? And can those learnings improve the model for the next program?

If you’re just handing over predictions and never seeing what happens in the lab, then I think the criticism has real weight. You don’t have much of a feedback loop. But partnerships can also be a way to generate feedback across more targets and experimental settings than you could cover yourself.

So I wouldn’t infer either the presence or absence of a data moat from the word “partnership.” I’d look at the rights, the quality of the experimental feedback, and whether that feedback produces a compounding improvement in the model. That’s the substantive question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that argument conflates exclusive ownership of data with a data moat. The question is: what does the partnership let you learn, and can that learning compound?

If you’re just handing a partner predictions and never seeing the experimental results, then the criticism has teeth. You don’t have a feedback loop. But if the relationship gives you access to outcomes—what worked, what failed, under what conditions—you can improve the model and make the next round of experiments more informative.

The important caveat is that those rights aren’t automatic. Can you train on the results? Can you use what you learn across partnerships? How consistently do you get feedback? Those details determine whether you’re building a compounding advantage or doing a series of isolated projects.

So I wouldn’t say partnerships imply no data moat. I’d ask whether the partnerships actually close that learning loop.
